Extremely urgent alerts are indicated by a RED warning light on the Caution/Warning panel. Warnings are also accompanied by a Master Warning light located directly in front of the pilot and copilot..t.

Examples of warnings include fire, hydraulic pressure failure, generator failure, and other critical system failures. Warnings must be attended to immediately to ensure the safety of the aircraft and passengers.

If a system failure is not critical to safe flight, the pilots are notified with a Caution. Examples of cautions include Autopilot disengage, Fuel transfer pressure low, and Icing Conditions. Cautions need attention but do not require immediate action.

Advisories are also indicated on the Caution/Warning system. Advisories indicate a condition is set but has no effect on the safety of the aircraft. Advisory examples are Parking Brake Set, Auxiliary Power Unit On, and Fuel Transfer in Progress.action.

Other Caution and Warning systems include the Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS) and the Traffic/Collision Avoidance System (TCAS). These systems are independent of the Caution/Warning panel and usually sound an audible alarm.

The GPWS warns the pilot if the aircraft is getting too close to the ground with the landing gear in the up position. A digital voice prompts the pilot to take action while an alarm sounds.l and usually sound an audible alarm.

TheTCAS system alerts the pilots of any aircraft that comes too close to their aircraft. The system is based on speed and time. It provides an audible caution when an aircraft is approaching from any angle, and a voice/alarm when the aircraft is on a collision course...

INTRODUCTION TO TROUBLESHOOTING.
DISCUSSION

As an Aviation Maintenance Technician or Avionics Technician, your main job is fault isolation and repair of aircraft systems. When an aircraft taxis up to the gate, or returns to the hangar, 90% of the discrepancies keeping it out of service will be systems related...

Returning the aircraft to service quickly and efficiently will reflect on your abilities as a technician. The best technicians are good troubleshooters, and good troubleshooting comes from having a systematic approach to fault finding...
* Know how and when to use test equipment.
* Recognize a properly configured system.
* Recognize how a system's performance changes in a "hostile" environment...
Before you can troubleshoot a system, you must first be aware of a few important concepts.

Understanding how the system works requires you to know the purpose of the system and all of the components associated with the system. If you are unsure of how a system works, there are manuals and training courses that explain its configuration and normal operation...

Test equipment can be a technician's best friends. Learning how to use them is important, but is just as important to know when to use them. Simple test equipment includes multimeters, oscilloscopes, logic probes, and meggers...

Recognizing proper system outputs is important to determining if a system is working properly. System outputs can be in the form of a voltage that drives an indicator, lights a lamp, or moves a control surface..
An output could also be in the form of signals that are sent along a data bus or wire to another system. In this configuration, one system's output is another system's input.

For a system to work properly, all of its inputs must be working properly. A good working knowledge of the correct inputs to a system will help determine if the system is faulty or perhaps one of its inputs is faulty...

To determine if a system fault truly exists, you must be certain that the system is configured correctly for the desired outcome. Knobs or switches set incorrectly, improper power application, and improper signals applied will give a false failure...

Finally, it is important to know how systems operate when they are in hostile environments. For example, thunderstorms impair some communications systems, and we have all heard of the problems navigation systems experience from the in-flight use of certain electronic devices...

Many schools teach troubleshooting processes with a varying number of steps, but basically, each process is the same. They all define the problem, verify, fault isolate, repair, operational check, and clear the problem. The flow chart shows how this is accomplished...

There are two phases to the Define the Problem step; receive the discrepancy and interview the operator. Some systems require the aircraft to be flying or running in order to gather information about the problem. If the aircraft is still airborne, you can interview the crew to aid in your troubleshooting. This can save you time and the company money...

Once the aircraft is on the ground, a valuable resource in defining the problem is the crew. Be sure to interview the crew to obtain as many details about the problem as you can. As with any interview, you must use your best listening skills so you don't miss important information..

The crew might provide information that was not written up such as; how they were operating the system at the time of the problem, other symptoms they may not have written up, or environmental conditions at the time of the problem...

The next step in the system troubleshooting process is Verifying the Problem. To properly perform this step, you must be familiar with the system. Verifying the problem requires visual inspection, system operation, and observation...
A visual inspection of the suspected system is accomplished to rule out any obvious faults. It is also used to identify any faults that could cause additional damage to the aircraft or crew.
* Circuit breaker - Check circuit protectors for tripping,
overheating, security, corrosion, and mechanical condition
* Switch - Check for position, security, arcing, corrosion,
* Equipment - Check for overheating, burnt odor, corrosion,
* Mechanical Linkage - Check for binding, interference,
distortion, excessive play, missing hardware, and
* Wires - Check for overheating, chafing, corrosion, breakage
* Lines & Connections - Check for leaking, damage, and security.

Many aircraft systems have Built In Test Equipment (BITE) indicators on the system control box that turn color or pop a flag when the system malfunctions. Visually check the BITE Indicators when troubleshooting to help isolate potential faults.....................................................
* Identifies good and bad outputs of the system
* Identifies what inputs could cause the bad outputs

If the visual inspection does not reveal any obvious results, an operational check of the system is completed next. Applicable publications and manuals should be used to guide you through the systems proper operation. The manuals will provide the following information.* Test equipment required * How to operate the test equipment * Identifies good and bad outputs of the system * Identifies what inputs could cause the bad outputs * Provides operating limits * Provides operating procedures

Many aircraft systems have self-tests built into their systems that provide readouts, indications, or software downloads revealing faulty conditions or components. A good troubleshooter will run the self tests while performing the operational checks...

If you are unable to duplicate the problem, use the information obtained in the interview to determine if the problem may have been operator induced. Not all problems can be duplicated on the ground so be careful not to jump to this conclusion too quickly...

DEFINITION
OPERATOR INDUCED - An operator induced fault is one in which the operator either set the system up incorrectly or attempted to operate the system beyond its designed capabilities.

Once you have verified that a problem exists, the next step in the troubleshooting process is Problem Isolation. When isolating faults you basically become a system detective. Your job is to eliminate each component that is functioning correctly, and zero in on the suspect faulty item...

Like a detective, you have tools to help you in your search for the problem. The tools include block diagrams, test equipment, publications, component history, your own senses, and, of course, system experts...

Knowledge of a system's functional block diagram is fundamental to successful problem solving. Block diagrams show the signal flow of the system as well as inputs and outputs. Remember our example? That was a block diagram....

Test equipment is an important part of your troubleshooting toolbox. Test equipment is used to isolate a system down to the failed component or wire. For example, multimeters can perform continuity checks on wires and measure system voltages and current...

At this point, you believe you have fixed the problem. Before you sign off the discrepancy, you must complete a final Operational Check. The Operational Check is performed to verify that the problem is fixed and to ensure no additional problems exist. If a new problem has been identified, you must start the process over.....

The PC130-741 card simulates our aircraft's Power Distribution System. This card has a few logic functions that are important to know.
If a system requires two signals to operate, it is called an AND system and has a unique symbol. All input signals must be present and valid for an AND system to operate.
If a system can operate with either signal or both signals present, it is called an OR system. In an OR system, only one signal needs to be valid for the system to operate.

The last logic system is the NOT system. If no signals are present, this system operates. If any signal is valid, this system is off. You will see why this is an important system to have on an aircraft...

If either the #1 OR #2 Main Busses are operating, the Start Bus will operate and both #1 and #2 Engine Start systems will operate. The Start Bus is an OR system..

The Non-Essential Bus requires both #1 AND #2 Main bus inputs for it to operate. If either the #1 or #2 Main busses fail, the Non-Essential bus system and all its subsystems will quit operating which reduces the load on the operating Main bus. The Non-Essential Bus is an AND system....
